newsitem.title: USA: US May payrolls underscore labor market tightness.
newsitem.headline: US May payrolls underscore labor market tightness.

text.p: Another drop in the unemployment rate and strong upward revisions to the March and April payrolls figures underscored the extreme tightness and continued strength of the U.S. labor market on Friday.

Though worrisome signs of wage inflation were absent from the report, economists said the figures provided further evidence that the U.S. economy is operating at full capacity and that inflation may well be around the corner.
"We're pushing the envelope here," said Gary Thayer, senior economist at A.G. Edwards & Sons Inc in St. Louis.
"So far the unemployment rate keeps coming down without a lot of wage inflation but it's somewhere out there and I think the risks are definitely increasing."
The Labor Department reported on Friday that 138,000 jobs were added to the U.S. economy in May, substantially lower than the 219,000 expected by Wall Street economists.
But the report also showed another downtick in the unemployment rate, which now stands at a 23-1/2 year low of 4.8 percent.

A sharp upward revision to the April jobs number, which was revised from a gain of 142,000 to a heady advance of 323,000, and a solid 43,000 upward revision to the March figure also demonstrated that the weakness in May's headline figure was deceiving.
Given the revisions, Labor Department reported payrolls had grown at an average rate of 252,000 per month in the first four months of 1997, sharply up from 213,500 last month.
"The huge upward revision to April suggests the May number may only be a temporary slowdown in payroll increases," said David Jones, chief economist at Aubrey G. Lanston & Co Inc.
New Bureau of Labor Statistics seasonal adjustment factors, released last Friday, probably depressed the May number, economists said.
And many predicted that strength in other areas of the report could sway the Federal Reserve toward tightening monetary policy again at their upcoming meeting in early July.

"Our view is that the argument around the (Federal Open Market Committee) table in July will be more heated and we think a rate increase is more likely now the report is out," said James Padinha, economist at Briefing.com, an internet-based financial service.
After release of the jobs figures, Labor Department economist Harvey Hamel told Reuters Financial Television that the report had contained signs of accelerating wage gains.

Average hourly earnings rose a palatable four cents, or 0.3 percent in May, while the previous month's figure was revised up to a 0.1 percent advance against an originally reported 0.1 percent decline.

So far, an upcreep in wage gains and continued strong jobs growth has failed to filter through to consumer prices. But many economists feel it is only a matter of time before inflation will become a problem again.
Economists put the year-over-year wage increase at roughly 3.8 percent -- not in and of itself a worrisome figure.
But with joblessness so low, a self-described "preemptive" Federal Reserve could see the need to fend off inflation pressures before they manifest themselves.
"This report doesn't show that the low unemployment rate today is causing a problem today but it does show that the risks are up," said Thayer.
